title: Meta's Muse Gadgets: Open-Source AI Hardware and What It Means for Developers
excerpt: Meta has introduced Muse Gadgets, an open-source project letting developers build custom hardware powered by the personal AI agent Muse.
metaDescription: Discover Meta's Muse Gadgets open-source project. Learn what the new AI hardware, firmware, and SDK mean for developers, tinkerers, and businesses.
content:
Meta is pushing its personal AI ecosystem out of the browser and into the physical world. TechCrunch recently reported that the company launched **Muse Gadgets**, an open-source project that lets developers build custom hardware connected to the Muse AI agent. It's a clear step away from pure software and toward physical automation.

## The announcement

The Muse agent—known for handling chores like booking travel and filling out forms—is now open to hardware hackers. The new open-source setup gives you the low-level foundation you need to build physical devices that talk directly to the assistant.

* **Open-Source Firmware and SDK:** Meta provides open-source firmware and a Linux software development kit (SDK) for custom builds.
* **Hardware Flexibility:** You can use cheap hobbyist boards like a Raspberry Pi or an ESP32 to hook Muse up to displays, buttons, sensors, and actuators.
* **Project Blueprints:** Meta's early ideas include adding a color e-ink display to Muse or loading the software onto a stick that plugs straight into a TV's HDMI port.
* **Community Support:** There's a dedicated Discord channel for developers and hardware tinkerers testing out the platform.

## What changed

Muse started as a software assistant for consumers, but Meta is expanding its reach quickly. This hardware push runs right alongside new enterprise tools aimed at corporate setups.

* **Muse Home Link:** Nat Friedman, head of product at Meta's Superintelligence Labs, showed off a USB-C gadget that connects Muse to home networks, smart speakers, and TVs. Meta built 5,000 of these and gave them away to Muse subscribers.
* **Muse for Small Business:** Meta launched a free tier with usage limits that plugs Muse straight into tools like Shopify, Dropbox, and Slack.
* **Meta Enterprise Platform:** A new business unit built to push Meta's AI tools to corporate customers and small shops.

## What it means for you

For developers and product teams, these updates point straight toward agentic AI that interacts with physical spaces. While models like [Google's Gemini 4 Argon: What You Need to Know About the New Frontier AI Model](/blog/googles-gemini-4-argon-frontier-ai-model-released) chase raw intelligence, Meta is betting on practical accessibility.

* **Rapid Prototyping:** The new SDK and firmware mean your team can prototype ambient computing devices without writing an AI agent from scratch.
* **Enterprise Integration:** Small businesses wanting to automate workflows can now plug straight into Slack, Shopify, and Dropbox via Meta's business tier.
* **Community-Driven Innovation:** With Discord support and cheap board compatibility (like ESP32 and Raspberry Pi), developer hubs—including teams right here in India—can test edge-AI hardware without spending a fortune.

## How to prepare

Moving from software to hardware-integrated AI takes a bit of planning. If you lead a technical team, it's worth looking at how physical interfaces might fit into your current products.

* **Explore the SDK and Firmware:** Check out Meta's open-source firmware and Linux SDK docs to see how external devices talk to Muse.
* **Experiment with Low-Cost Boards:** Grab an ESP32 or a Raspberry Pi to test simple sensor or display hookups on your workbench.
* **Engage the Community:** Jump into the official Meta Discord to swap troubleshooting tips with other hardware hackers and track early builds.

## The takeaway

Meta's Muse Gadgets show that personal AI agents are breaking past phone screens and browser windows. By dropping open-source firmware, Linux SDKs, and hardware blueprints, Meta wants developers to experiment with ambient, agent-driven hardware. For product teams and technical builders, now is the time to see where physical computing and agentic workflows cross paths in your next build.
